title: Chinese AI short dramas surge in South Korea as users near 5 million
text:
Chinese AI short dramas surge in South Korea as users near 5 million - CHOSUNBIZ 
 2026년 11월 18일(수) Industry Finance Real Estate IT Retail Science Policy Society International Entertainment Culture Sports English IT Chinese AI short dramas surge in South Korea as users near 5 million 
 Five Chinese platforms now account for roughly 80% of Korea's 5.07 million short‑drama users, with NetShort leading monthly installs at 750,000 
 입력 2026.11.18. 06:00 조선비즈 구글 검색 먼저 보기 
 Short-drama content provided on the short-form drama platform DramaBox, operated in Singapore by Beijing-based content company Dianzhong Technology (Dianzhong Technology). /Courtesy of DramaBox website As short-form drama, with plots that race forward in under a minute to heighten immersion, gains popularity, users of Korea's short-drama apps recently topped 5 million. The user base has nearly tripled in a year, and Chinese short dramas made with artificial intelligence (AI) are sweeping the top of the charts, expanding their influence.
 According to market research firm WiseApp·Retail on the 18th, the combined monthly active users (MAU) of 10 major short-drama apps in Korea came to about 5.07 million last month. That was up 197.4% from October last year (1.7 million).
 By monthly users, the top five short-drama apps were all Chinese platforms. China's DramaBox ranked No. 1 with 1.19 million, followed by NetShort (1.12 million), FreeReels (760,000), and DramaWave (680,000). ReelShort, run by U.S.-based Crazy Maple Studio, placed fifth with 500,000, but because Chinese publisher COL Group holds a 49.24% stake as the largest shareholder, it is effectively a Chinese platform.
 Monthly active user (MAU) rankings for major short-form drama apps among Korean smartphone users (Android+iOS) as of last month /Courtesy of ChatGPT Next, Vigloo, a Korean short-drama platform run by Spoon Labs, which is backed by Krafton, had 400,000 users for sixth place, and Lezhin Snack under Lezhin Entertainment ranked seventh with 170,000. Chinese short-drama apps accounted for about 80% of all users.
 Short dramas are ultra-short video content, about 1–2 minutes per episode. They are typically serialized drama-style shows that continue into the next episode, running a total of 50–100 episodes. Most plots are high-intensity, salacious "makjang stories" that deliver quick dopamine hits—romance, affairs, conglomerate heirs, revenge, and secret births.
 Vigloo says the main audience for short dramas in Korea is women 35 and older, who make up more than half of viewers. A company employee in her 40s who often watches short dramas in spare moments said, "The plots are so over the top that I can watch without thinking, and because they're short, they go down easy."
 Chinese short dramas also stood out in new app installs in Korea. According to app analytics platform Mobile Index, the Chinese short-drama app NetShort logged 750,000 new installs last month, ranking No. 1 in the entertainment category. It far outpaced downloads for streaming platforms Tving (470,000), Coupang Play (310,000), and Netflix (290,000).
 During the same period, Korean mobile (iOS+Android) users newly downloaded FreeReels 420,000 times, DramaBox 390,000, ReelShort 310,000, and DramaWave 290,000. New installs for five Chinese short-drama apps in October alone approached 2.16 million.
 Short dramas are also making inroads on traditional video platforms such as YouTube. YouTube says short-drama views on its platform surpassed 6.5 billion in the first half of this year, up 50% from the first half of last year. Demand in Korea has grown even faster. On YouTube Korea, views of short-drama videos surged more than 130% from July last year to July this year. Watch time more than doubled in the same period.
 YouTube said, "As more short-drama series deliver rapid pacing and immersive stories, our serialized content is rapidly evolving around vertical video."
 The short-drama market does not yet have a clear No. 1, and numerous platforms are vying for the lead. Chinese platforms such as DramaBox and ReelShort stand out because they have an overwhelming number of titles and churn out new releases quickly.
 Some Chinese short dramas feature live actors, but many are produced with AI, allowing low-cost mass production. According to Xinhua News Agency, the production cost for high-quality AI-made short dramas is about one-tenth that of live-action short dramas with real actors. A roughly 100-episode run can be finished in three days, so production time is short as well. Chinese platforms rapidly create provocative short dramas with AI and keep users engaged by continuously generating new shows based on the topics they like.
 Some argue that Chinese short-drama apps airing explicit content fall into a gray area for youth protection and need tighter regulation. In October, Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Lee Jeong-heon said at the National Assembly's Science. ICT. Broadcasting. and Communications Committee audit that DramaBox and DramaWave, whose operators are based in Singapore, were left off the list of entities required to appoint a youth-protection officer. "Sexually explicit short-drama content and ads are spreading, but the number of related review cases is zero," he said, calling for fixes to the system.
